artiest/chano-pozo.text: Luciano 'Chano' Pozo grew up in Havana, where he was a well-known conga player, dancer and composer for the carnival. From his youth he knew the rhythms and chants of Afro-Cuban religion. In 1947 he moved to New York, where Mario Bauzá introduced him to Dizzy Gillespie. Gillespie took him into his big band. In September 1947 they played at Carnegie Hall, and in December they recorded Manteca, a piece that Pozo and Gillespie conceived together. Pozo hardly spoke any English and taught the jazz musicians his rhythms by singing them. It was the first time a conga played such a central role in a jazz orchestra. In December 1948 he was shot dead in a bar in Harlem.
artiest/chano-pozo.listen: Follow the conga in the introduction to Manteca: that is where it all begins.

artiest/charanjit-singh.text:
Charanjit Singh was born on 15 December 1940 in Mumbai and died on 5 July 2015. He was an Indian musician and composer who worked for decades in the Bollywood music industry. As a session musician he played bass, keyboards, guitar and synthesizer on hundreds of soundtracks. He worked closely with composers such as R. D. Burman, S. D. Burman and Laxmikant-Pyarelal and toured with the singer Kishore Kumar. Colleagues often called on him when a modern sound was wanted.

He also released records under his own name. With a wedding band he recorded instrumental versions of film songs, sometimes with steel guitar. In 1981 he made electronic arrangements of the soundtrack of Silsila. His best-known work is Synthesizing: Ten Ragas to a Disco Beat from 1982, listed in the album lists as Ten Ragas to a Disco Beat. On it he combined Indian classical ragas with electronic disco. For this he used a TR-808 drum machine and a TB-303 bass synthesizer, devices that would later become the foundation of acid house.

That album went unnoticed for a long time. Music journalists later pointed out that it may be the earliest example of acid house, and some call Singh the father of that genre. His story shows that dance music did not arise only in Chicago, Detroit or Europe. In the Bollywood studios of Mumbai, too, people were already experimenting with the machines that would later conquer the clubs.
artiest/charanjit-singh.listen: Listen to a track from Ten Ragas to a Disco Beat and notice the drum machine and the buzzing bass synthesizer. Try to hear how the melody follows an Indian raga while the rhythm sounds like disco.

artiest/charles-aznavour.text:
Charles Aznavour was born in Paris in 1924 as Shahnour Vaghinag Aznavourian, in a family of Armenian immigrants. His parents had a small Armenian restaurant in the rue de la Huchette, a meeting place for actors and musicians. He became a French-Armenian singer, songwriter, actor and diplomat. In a career of more than seventy years he recorded more than twelve hundred songs, in many languages, and wrote more than a thousand songs for himself and others. His first albums, Charles Aznavour chante Charles Aznavour, appeared from 1953. In 1965 La bohème was released.

His voice was a tenor with a distinctive vibrato: clear in the high register, raw and deep in the low notes. He was called the French Frank Sinatra, and the critic Stephen Holden called him a French pop god. Jean Cocteau, who gave him a role in Le Testament d'Orphée in 1960, said that despair was not popular for Aznavour. After the earthquake in Armenia in 1988 he founded, with Lévon Sayan, the organisation Aznavour for Armenia, and from 1994 he was Armenia's ambassador to UNESCO.

Aznavour was regarded as one of the greatest songwriters of all time. His chansons tell small stories full of longing, loss and love, with a cinematic eye. In 2017 he received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, and he performed until shortly before his death in 2018.
artiest/charles-aznavour.listen: Listen to La bohème. Notice how the song begins as a quiet story about a painter in Montmartre and how the voice and the accompaniment gradually grow larger.

artiest/charles-bernstein.text:
Charles Bernstein is an American composer of film and television music, born in 1943 in Minneapolis. His mother was a pianist. He studied music at the Juilliard School and is not related to Elmer Bernstein or Leonard Bernstein. He wrote his first film music for the documentary Czechoslovakia 1968 from 1969, a film without spoken commentary, in which only music and a few sound effects told the story. The documentary won an Oscar.

In the 1970s he scored low-budget films and, from White Lightning in 1973, starring Burt Reynolds, larger Hollywood productions too. Gator, Mr. Majestyk and Love at First Bite followed, for which he also wrote the dance music. In the 1980s he wrote music for horror films such as The Entity, Cujo, April Fool's Day and Deadly Friend. On the advice of his agent he met Wes Craven, who had him write the music for A Nightmare on Elm Street from 1984, of which Main Title is the opening music.

Bernstein also wrote music for documentaries, one of which, Maya Lin: A Strong Clear Vision, won an Oscar, and for television films such as Sadat. He won a Daytime Emmy and was twice nominated for a Primetime Emmy. His work shows how film music can create a frightening atmosphere with simple means, such as synthesizer sounds that repeat ominously.
artiest/charles-bernstein.listen: Listen to Main Title from A Nightmare on Elm Street. Notice the electronic sounds and how the music builds tension without needing a real melody.

artiest/charles-gerhardt.text:
Charles Gerhardt (1927 to 1999) was an American conductor, producer and arranger. He grew up in Little Rock, Arkansas, and studied, among other things, piano and composition. He began at RCA Victor as a technician, where he transferred old 78 rpm records by Enrico Caruso to tape. Later he worked at Westminster Records. In 1960 he began producing records for RCA Victor and Reader's Digest. Together with the Decca sound engineer Kenneth Wilkinson he worked on thousands of recording sessions, often in London.

In 1964, together with the violinist Sidney Sax, he put together an orchestra of the best London musicians. In 1970 it officially became the National Philharmonic Orchestra. With that orchestra Gerhardt recorded the Classic Film Scores series for RCA from 1972 to 1978, fourteen LPs. It began with music by Erich Wolfgang Korngold and went on to Max Steiner, Miklós Rózsa, Franz Waxman, Alfred Newman, Dimitri Tiomkin and Bernard Herrmann. Gerhardt prepared the scores with great care and recorded in Kingsway Hall. In 1978 came a recording of music by John Williams from Star Wars and Close Encounters of the Third Kind.

Gerhardt also made pop-oriented records. With the flautist James Galway he recorded, among other things, Annie's Song, an album that reached the top three in Britain. His importance lies chiefly in film music. He gave symphonic film scores from the Hollywood of the 1930s and 1940s a second life on record, at a time when that music was hardly being played any more.
artiest/charles-gerhardt.listen: Listen to the recording of music from Star Wars on Music From John Williams' Classic Film Scores. Notice how a full symphony orchestra plays the themes with plenty of colour and volume, as in a concert hall.

artiest/charles-k-harris.text:
Charles Kassel Harris (1867 to 1930) was an American songwriter and one of the pioneers of Tin Pan Alley. He was born in Poughkeepsie in New York State, in a Jewish family of ten children, and grew up in Saginaw and Milwaukee. He began as a banjo player and in 1885 wrote his first song, Since Maggie Learned To Skate, for a play. In his long career he published more than three hundred songs. Admirers called him the king of the tearjerkers.

His big breakthrough came in 1892 with After the Ball, the story of an old man who tells his niece about his lost love. John Philip Sousa played the song at the 1893 world's fair in Chicago, after which sheet-music sales in the 1890s rose above five million copies. Break the News to Mother followed in 1897, about a dying soldier, and in 1899 A Rabbi's Daughter. His sentimental songs were sung on stages and in music halls, but the rural bands of the South also took them over. Charlie Poole and The Carter Family recorded songs of his, such as Hello Central, Give Me Heaven from 1901.

Harris later wrote for musicals, among others with Oscar Hammerstein, and in 1906 published the book How to Write a Popular Song. His work shows how the music industry around 1900 revolved around sheet music: a good song spread via pianos at home, long before the record took its place.
artiest/charles-k-harris.listen: Listen to a recording of After the Ball and notice the waltz time and the narrative, sentimental verse. Try to hear how the chorus was made for singing along at the piano at home.

artiest/charles-king.text:
Charles King was an American singer and actor from the early days of sound film. He became known on Broadway and was given a leading role in The Broadway Melody from 1929, one of the first big musical films with sound. The film was about two sisters in the theatre world of New York and let the audience hear for the first time how popular songs from the theatre could sound on the silver screen.

The title song The Broadway Melody, written by Nacio Herb Brown and Arthur Freed, was sung in the film by King. The song is an example of the kind of theatre song that was popular in the late 1920s, with a cheerful rhythm, a smooth melody and lyrics about the glamorous life on Broadway. The film won an Oscar for best picture and gave the film musical genre a flying start.

In pop history King stands above all for the moment when the pop song and the film found each other, and for the way songs from films acquired an audience of their own in the 1930s.
artiest/charles-king.listen: Listen to The Broadway Melody. Notice the clear, theatrical singing style and the cheerful accompaniment that makes the song instantly recognisable as music from a revue.

artiest/charles-lloyd.text:
Charles Lloyd was born in 1938 in Memphis and is an American jazz musician and composer. He plays mainly tenor saxophone and flute. In Memphis he grew up with blues, gospel and jazz, and as a teenager he played with blues artists such as Howlin' Wolf and B.B. King. In 1956 he left for Los Angeles to study music. In 1960 he became music director of Chico Hamilton's group, after which he played in Cannonball Adderley's sextet. In 1964 he signed with Columbia and began recording under his own name, with Discovery! and Of Course, Of Course.

In 1966 he formed his quartet in New York with the pianist Keith Jarrett, the bassist Cecil McBee and the drummer Jack DeJohnette. Their live album Forest Flower, recorded at the Monterey Jazz Festival in 1966, was one of the most successful jazz records of those years. It also attracted rock fans and hippies. The quartet toured America and Europe and in 1967 even played in Estonia and Leningrad. Lloyd incorporated elements from other cultures into his music at an early stage.

In the 1970s he withdrew and played, among other things, with The Beach Boys, both in the studio and on tour. From 1981 he returned to jazz. From 1989 he recorded for ECM, beginning with Fish Out of Water. His sound is open and lyrical. Lloyd shows how jazz in the 1960s found an audience outside the jazz clubs, and how that world touched pop music.
artiest/charles-lloyd.listen: Listen to Forest Flower and notice Lloyd's flute playing and Keith Jarrett's piano playing. Try to hear how the group grows from calm and open to a wild, rhythmic eruption.

artiest/charles-mackerras.text:
Sir Charles Mackerras (1925 to 2010) was an Australian conductor who spent most of his adult life in London. He was born in Schenectady in the United States to Australian parents and grew up in Sydney. As a child he played violin and flute, and at sixteen he studied oboe, piano and composition at the Sydney conservatory. Later he became an authority on the operas of Janáček and Mozart, and on the comic operas of Gilbert and Sullivan. Czech music in general also had his special attention. He made many recordings for the Czech label Supraphon.

His career took him through many houses. From 1954 to 1956 he was chief conductor of the BBC Concert Orchestra, from 1965 to 1969 he led the opera in Hamburg and from 1970 to 1977 the English National Opera. In 1980 he was the first non-Briton to conduct the Last Night of the Proms. From 1982 to 1985 he was the first Australian to be chief conductor of the Sydney Symphony Orchestra. He then worked at the Welsh National Opera, where his Janáček productions in particular were praised. Records released include Finlandia: Music of Grieg and Sibelius in 1959, The Indian Queen in 1966 and 1812 Overture in 1970.

Mackerras was known as a conductor who combined thorough research with lively playing. He looked for the original sources of a work and tried to make that music sound the way the composer intended. His influence on British operatic life is described as great in the Grove dictionary.
artiest/charles-mackerras.listen: Listen to his recording of 1812 Overture and notice the way the orchestra works from a quiet beginning towards a loud ending with cannons and bells. Try to hear where the melodies alternate.

artiest/charles-mingus.text: Charles Mingus grew up in Watts, Los Angeles, and was a bassist, composer and bandleader. Duke Ellington was his great example; as a boy he heard East St. Louis Toodle-Oo and in 1953 he briefly played in Ellington's orchestra. He played with Louis Armstrong, Lionel Hampton and Charlie Parker. In his Jazz Workshop he taught his musicians the pieces by ear, so that they could remain free. His music blends gospel, blues, bebop and free passages. Mingus was combative: in Fables of Faubus he mocked the governor of Arkansas, who had refused Black schoolchildren entry to a school. He wrote Goodbye Pork Pie Hat in memory of Lester Young.
artiest/charles-mingus.listen: Notice the bass: not merely accompaniment, but a voice that joins the conversation and pushes.

artiest/charles-pitts.text:
Charles Pitts, nicknamed Skip, was born in 1947 in Washington D.C. and died in 2012. He was an American soul and blues guitarist, best known for his wah-wah style. He learned to play the guitar on the street at the age of eleven, and received tips there from his neighbour Bo Diddley. His uncle had a hotel next to the Howard Theater, where he met musicians such as James Brown and Otis Redding. At seventeen he played on Rainbow '65 by Gene Chandler. He then became guitarist and bandleader with Wilson Pickett, where he accompanied Pickett and Sam & Dave. In 1969 he joined The Isley Brothers and devised the recognisable riff of It's Your Thing.

In 1970 he moved to Memphis to play in Isaac Hayes's band. A year later he devised the wah-wah intro of Theme From Shaft, a song that earned Hayes an Oscar. He stayed with Hayes for more than thirty years, until Hayes's death in 2008, and played on records, in the film Truck Turner and on the South Park soundtrack. At Stax Records he worked as a session musician for, among others, Rufus Thomas and Albert King. In 1998 he was a co-founder of The Bo-Keys.

Pitts's guitar parts later returned in hip hop. Dr. Dre, the Beastie Boys and Massive Attack sampled his riffs from Stax recordings. His playing forms a line from soul to funk, and thus also to the rhythms of later pop music.
artiest/charles-pitts.listen: Listen to the beginning of Theme From Shaft and notice the guitar with wah-wah that opens the song. Try to hear how the guitar plays a tight, rhythmic pattern that sounds almost like a second drummer.

artiest/charles-williams.text:
Charles Williams (1893 to 1978) was a British composer and conductor who wrote music for more than fifty films. He was born in London as Isaac Cozerbreit. He began as a freelance violinist in theatres, cinemas and symphony orchestras and then studied composition at the Royal Academy of Music. In 1933 he joined Gaumont British Films as a composer, where he remained until 1939. After the Second World War he became conductor of the Queen's Hall Light Orchestra and later formed his own Concert Orchestra. Much of his film music was reused as stock music and therefore went uncredited.

His best-known work falls under light music, the so-called mood music. His first success was the march Blue Devils, which he wrote in 1926 for the opening of the Odeon in Kensington. Many of his short orchestral pieces became signature tunes for radio and television in the 1950s. Devil's Galop was the tune of the radio serial Dick Barton, The Young Ballerina accompanied the famous BBC interlude The Potter's Wheel, and Girls in Grey became known as the tune of BBC Television Newsreel. In Australia, Majestic Fanfare from 1935 served for years as the signature tune of the ABC news.

Williams showed how a short, easily remembered melody could become a fixture of daily life. Many people knew his music without knowing his name. In this way you heard his compositions on radio and TV in the 1950s, even if nobody would have described them as pop music.
artiest/charles-williams.listen: Listen to Devil's Galop and notice the fast, driving tempo and the short melody that repeats. Try to hear why this piece was suited to a thrilling radio story.

artiest/charley-patton.text:
Charley Patton, also spelled Charlie, was probably born in April 1891 in Hinds County, Mississippi, near the town of Edwards. He lived most of his life in Sunflower County, in the Mississippi Delta. His ancestry is uncertain: he is said to have been of Black, white and Native American descent. In 1897 his family moved to Dockery Plantation near Ruleville, a cotton farm with a sawmill. There Patton developed his style, under the influence of Henry Sloan, who had a new way of playing that is now regarded as an early form of the blues.

Patton is called the father of the Delta blues by many and inspired most Delta blues musicians. Pony Blues from 1929 is among his early recordings. He played deep blues, but also hillbilly songs, nineteenth-century ballads and other dance music for Black and white audiences, with equal ease. He was popular throughout the South, performed in Chicago every year and in New York in 1934. Unlike many blues musicians of his time he did not travel around, but played regular engagements on plantations and in bars.

He was known for his showmanship: sometimes he played with the guitar on his knees, behind his head or behind his back. He was small, but his raw voice could reportedly be heard without amplification from five hundred metres away. Patton died on 28 April 1934. The musicologist Robert Palmer counted him among the most important American musicians of the twentieth century.
artiest/charley-patton.listen: Listen to Pony Blues. Notice the rough, hoarse voice and the rhythmic guitar, which seems to be accompaniment and percussion at the same time.

artiest/charli-xcx.text:
Charli XCX, real name Charlotte Emma Aitchison, is a British singer, songwriter and actress, born in 1992. She began posting songs on Myspace in 2008 and then found her way into the London rave scene. In 2010 she signed with Asylum Records. In 2012 she co-wrote and sang on Icona Pop's I Love It, her first number 1 in the United Kingdom. In 2014 she featured on Iggy Azalea's Fancy and released Boom Clap, her first solo top ten in the United States. Her debut album True Romance from 2013 fell short of expectations.

From 2015 she worked with producers around the British collective PC Music and her music took on a more experimental sound. She released Vroom Vroom in 2016 and the mixtapes Number 1 Angel and Pop 2 in 2017. Charli from 2019 included 1999 with Troye Sivan, and how i'm feeling now from 2020 was made during the coronavirus lockdown. Crash from 2022 became her first number 1 album in the United Kingdom. In 2024 came BRAT, containing 360, which was chosen best album of the year by, among others, Billboard and Rolling Stone and won three Grammys. It set off the so-called Brat Summer.

Besides her own work she co-wrote songs for others, such as Señorita by Shawn Mendes and Camila Cabello. She shows how pop music can be renewed with club sounds, distortion and a self-assured attitude.
artiest/charli-xcx.listen: Listen to 360. Notice the tight, electronic beat and the cool, almost indifferent singing, with which the song creates a club atmosphere.

artiest/charlie-byrd.text:
Charlie Byrd (1925 to 1999) was an American jazz guitarist who played a classical guitar with his fingers. He was born in Suffolk, Virginia, and as a child was given guitar lessons by his father. In the war he served in the American army and played in an army band in Paris. There he saw Django Reinhardt, who would remain his greatest influence. After the war he studied composition and jazz theory in New York, moved to Washington in 1950 and became a pupil of the classical guitarist Andrés Segovia. In 1957 he met the bassist Keter Betts, with whom he played for years. In 1959 they toured Europe with Woody Herman's band.

Byrd became best known for his band playing Brazilian music. Through his friend Felix Grant, a radio presenter, he got to know that music. In 1962 he recorded the album Jazz Samba with the saxophonist Stan Getz, which brought the bossa nova to a large audience in North America. He also made albums himself such as Latin Impressions and Charlie Byrd's Bossa Nova Once More! in 1963, and later Brazilian Byrd in 1966.

His sound is soft and intimate: a nylon-string guitar, a light bass and a supple rhythm. Byrd linked the classical guitar school with jazz and with Brazilian rhythms. In doing so he helped to spread a musical style from Rio in the United States, where the bossa nova became a fashion in 1962 and 1963.
artiest/charlie-byrd.listen: Listen to a track from Jazz Samba and notice the nylon-string guitar alongside Stan Getz's saxophone. Try to hear how the rhythm of the guitar carries the song, without the music becoming loud.

artiest/charlie-chaplin.text: Charlie Chaplin was born in London in 1889 and became world-famous in Hollywood with his tramp, the Little Tramp. When sound film arrived he went on making silent films, but he used sound to put his own music on them. City Lights (1931) has no audible dialogue, but does have a continuous orchestral score with sound effects. Chaplin did not write out his music himself: he hummed the melodies, and arrangers such as Arthur Johnston, Alfred Newman and David Raksin worked them out for orchestra. In Modern Times (1936) his voice is heard for the first time, in a song in gibberish. The love theme from that film became, with lyrics added in 1954, the song Smile. For Limelight (1952) he finally received an Oscar in 1973.
artiest/charlie-chaplin.listen: Notice how the music takes the place of the voice: simple, singing melodies carry the tender scenes, and short pieces with a character of their own follow the mood of the Tramp.

artiest/charlie-christian.text: Charlie Christian grew up in Oklahoma City and made the electric guitar a solo instrument. In 1939 the producer John Hammond brought him to Benny Goodman, in whose sextet he played for two years. With an amplifier the guitar could, for the first time, play as loud as a saxophone. Christian played long lines of eighth notes, like a horn player, with Lester Young as his example, and based himself on the chords. After his work with Goodman he went at night to Minton's Playhouse in Harlem, where he played with Thelonious Monk and Kenny Clarke; an amateur recorded a few sessions there in 1941. Christian had tuberculosis and died in 1942 at the age of 25.
artiest/charlie-christian.listen: Hear how the electric guitar plays lines like a saxophone.

artiest/charlie-haden.text: The bassist Charlie Haden grew up in Iowa and Missouri in a family that sang country music on the radio. In 1959 he played in Ornette Coleman's quartet, where his warm, simple bass lines connected the free melodies. In 1969 he founded the Liberation Music Orchestra with Carla Bley, which played songs from the Spanish Civil War and protest music. Song for Ché is a tribute to Che Guevara. Haden played in Keith Jarrett's quartet and later led Quartet West. With Pat Metheny he made Beyond the Missouri Sky (1996), a record of simple, quiet duets.
artiest/charlie-haden.listen: Notice the bass: few notes, but every note carries weight.

artiest/charlie-parker.text: Charlie Parker grew up in Kansas City, where as a teenager he listened in the clubs to the saxophonists of Count Basie. Lester Young was his great example; he learned his solos note for note from the record. In 1939 he went to New York for the first time. He then played with Jay McShann and Earl Hines, and worked out bebop with Dizzy Gillespie. Parker played fast, long lines on the alto saxophone, with unexpected accents and complicated harmony, but also with a deep feeling for the blues. His nickname was 'Bird'. His recordings for Savoy and Dial from 1945 to 1948 became the model for almost every later jazz musician. He was addicted to heroin and died in 1955 at the age of 34.
artiest/charlie-parker.listen: Try to follow a single line by Parker: how long does he keep going without taking a breath?

artiest/charly-lownoise.text:
Charly Lownoise is the stage name of Ramon Roelofs, a Dutch DJ and producer from The Hague, born in 1968. He began as a teenager as a DJ at school parties with a mobile disco. From 1989 he played in Hague clubs such as Sandokan, Tahiti and Marathon. Because he could not yet make a living from DJing, he also worked as a driver for a bank. In 1991 he broke through with Rave This Nation under the name RJ's Rule. Shortly afterwards he changed his name to Charly Lownoise. Under the name Fluxland he made a successful EP in 1993.

In 1992 he played for six weeks in a club in Mallorca and afterwards met Theo Nabuurs, better known as Mental Theo. They wanted to go in the same direction in house and continued as a duo: Charly Lownoise & Mental Theo. Their big breakthrough was Wonderful Days, a track with a sample of Help Get Me Some Help by Tony Ronald. It was the beginning of the popularity of happy hardcore in the Netherlands. Well-known tracks by the duo also include Stars and Live At London, and Revolution sounds in Alkmaar after a goal by AZ. The duo played their last show in 2022 in the Ziggo Dome.

After the duo Roelofs had successes in Germany with Topmodelz and Starsplash. His music consists of a high tempo, hard basses and cheerful, almost childlike melodies. In this way he belongs to the Dutch dance scene of the 1990s, in which gabber and happy hardcore grew into a popular culture of their own.
artiest/charly-lownoise.listen: Listen to Wonderful Days and notice the cheerful melody over a hard, fast rhythm. Try to hear where the sampled song by Tony Ronald returns in the track.

artiest/charly-lownoise-en-mental-theo.text:
Charly Lownoise & Mental Theo was a Dutch DJ duo that became known mainly for happy hardcore, and also made gabber and Eurodance. Charly Lownoise is the stage name of Ramon Roelofs, born in 1968 in The Hague, and Mental Theo is Theo Nabuurs, born in 1965 in Den Bosch. Roelofs began in 1989 as a DJ in a Hague discotheque and played a summer in Mallorca. His first production success came under the name R.J.'s Rule. In the early 1990s he met Nabuurs, also a DJ in Mallorca, and within two weeks they released their first single. Both contributed to the Thunderdome compilations.

In 1995 their most successful record appeared, the gold-certified Wonderful Days. The track uses a sample of Help Get Me Some Help by Tony Ronald. Nabuurs got the idea when he accidentally played the record at 45 rpm. Because Ronald's record company refused permission, they re-recorded the track with Albert West. It brought them international fame, and in 1995 they performed 325 times. Later albums include Charlottenburg and Old School Hardcore. Their track Revolution sounds like AZ scoring at home.

The duo gave their last performance on 30 July 2022 at the Ziggo Dome in Amsterdam. Worldwide they sold more than three million records. They show how Dutch hardcore of the 1990s combined cheerful melodies and hard beats.
artiest/charly-lownoise-en-mental-theo.listen: Listen to Wonderful Days. Notice the high, sped-up voice sample and how it dances over the fast, hard beat.

artiest/chas-mcdevitt-skiffle-group.text:
The Chas McDevitt Skiffle Group belonged to the wave of skiffle that swept through the United Kingdom in the 1950s. Skiffle is folk music with influences from American folk, blues, country, bluegrass and jazz, played on a mixture of ordinary and home-made or improvised instruments. The style comes from the United States, where jug bands in the South played blues and jazz on washboard, jug, washtub bass and comb and paper. In England skiffle became wildly popular in the 1950s, played by, among others, Lonnie Donegan, the Vipers Skiffle Group, Ken Colyer and Chas McDevitt.

British skiffle grew out of the post-war jazz scene, where people moved away from swing to traditional jazz. Lonnie Donegan sang and played guitar, accompanied by, among other things, a washboard and a tea-chest bass, and played American folk and blues songs, mainly from the repertoire of Lead Belly, in a lively style. The music was cheap to make, because anyone could start a group with a guitar, a washboard and a home-made bass. Freight Train from 1957 belongs to that time.

Skiffle was important for many musicians who later became known in other genres, such as the Quarrymen, the later Beatles, Tony Sheridan and Rory Gallagher. The style is regarded as an important stepping stone to the second British folk revival, the British blues boom and the British Invasion of American pop music.
artiest/chas-mcdevitt-skiffle-group.listen: Listen to Freight Train. Notice the simple accompaniment with acoustic guitar and the rhythm that imitates a moving train.

artiest/chavela-vargas.text: Chavela Vargas was born in Costa Rica and left for Mexico at seventeen. She sang rancheras, songs that usually sound with a full mariachi band, with only a guitar, and slowed them down into raw laments. Her first album appeared in 1961 with the support of José Alfredo Jiménez. The director Pedro Almodóvar, an admirer, supported her debut at Carnegie Hall in 2003, when she was 83.
artiest/chavela-vargas.listen: Listen to La Llorona: only guitar and voice, and long silences in which the words echo.

artiest/cheap-trick.text:
Cheap Trick is an American rock band from Rockford, Illinois, formed in 1973. The guitarist Rick Nielsen and the bassist Tom Petersson had previously played together in Fuse, with the drummer Bun E. Carlos. They chose the name Cheap Trick after Petersson, following a Slade concert, said that the group used all the cheap tricks in the book. In 1974 the singer Robin Zander joined. The band played for years in warehouses, bowling alleys and other venues in the Midwest before releasing their first album in 1977, Cheap Trick, followed by In Color.

In Japan the group caught on first. The live album At Budokan from 1979 broke them in the United States, partly thanks to the live-recorded I Want You to Want Me, which reached the top ten. That same year came Dream Police, their commercially most successful studio album. In the 1980s their popularity declined, until the power ballad The Flame from Lap of Luxury topped the American charts in 1988. Other well-known songs are Surrender, Voices and Can't Stop Fallin' into Love.

The music combines the guitar pop of the 1960s, the hard rock of the 1970s and the shorter, faster form of punk. It features hefty guitars beneath sweet melodies, with a singer who can both scream and sing softly. The group is regarded as a model for later power-pop bands and was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2016.
artiest/cheap-trick.listen: Listen to I Want You to Want Me in the live version from At Budokan and notice the screaming of the audience and the hefty guitar playing. Try to hear how a simple, sweet chorus is played hard and energetically.

artiest/cheb-hasni.text:
Cheb Hasni, whose real name was Hasni Chakroun, was an Algerian raï singer, born on 1 February 1968 in Oran into a working-class family. His father was a welder and his mother a housewife; he was one of seven children. He played football for the local club ASMO, but after an injury at fifteen he could not continue his sporting career. He had been interested in singing from an early age. His first real performance was at a wedding, where the Naoui brothers were playing and invited him to a well-known cabaret, La Guinguette.

He then recorded with the raï singer Chaba Zahouania. In 1987 they released Beraka, a song provocative by Algerian standards, with lyrics about drunken sex. It made Hasni famous and at the same time controversial among critics and fundamentalists. He married in 1987 and had a son in 1989. His wife Melouka inspired many of his greatest hits, such as Tal Ghyabek ya ghzali and El Bayda mon amour. Baïda Mon Amour is among them. Albums from his time are El Baraka from 1986 and Dak El Mahroum from 1992.

Hasni was called the King of Sentimental Music, and le rossignol du raï, the nightingale of raï. His peak came in the late 1980s and early 1990s, and he was popular throughout the Maghreb. He died on 29 September 1994, at the age of 26, and remains one of the most celebrated Algerian artists of the late twentieth century.
artiest/cheb-hasni.listen: Listen to Baïda Mon Amour. Notice the soft, plaintive singing and how the accompaniment with synthesizer and rhythm forms a whole that is danceable yet sad.

artiest/cheb-mami.text:
Cheb Mami is the stage name of Mohamed Khelifati, an Algerian raï singer and songwriter, born in 1966 in Saïda, a town in north-western Algeria. The word cheb is an honorific for raï musicians. He sings in Algerian Arabic, sometimes in other Arabic dialects and in French. In 1982, at sixteen, he came second in an Algerian TV talent contest. He then sang at weddings and released cassettes. In 1985 he moved to Paris, where he performed at raï festivals and met his manager Michel Levy. His military service in Algeria, where he performed on army bases, interrupted his rise for two years. In 1989 he returned to Paris and toured, among other places, the United States, Germany and the Netherlands.

On record he debuted with Prince of Raï in 1989, followed by Let Me Raï in 1990, Saïda in 1994 and Meli meli in 1998. His music blends Mediterranean and Western influences, including flamenco, Greek, Turkish and Latin American music, and his voice has an Andalusian tinge. He broke through internationally in 1999 with the vocals on Sting's Desert Rose, from the album Brand New Day. The duet appeared in charts all over the world and took him to American TV programmes and even the Super Bowl.

Cheb Mami belongs to the raï generation that reached the world from Algeria via Paris. He showed that pop music in Arabic could find a large audience. For many listeners his work with Sting is the first introduction to raï.
artiest/cheb-mami.listen: Listen to Desert Rose and notice the difference between Sting's Western singing and Cheb Mami's Arabic singing. Try to hear how his voice brings ornamentation and graceful turns into the chorus.

artiest/cheb-mami-en-k-mel.text:
Parisien du Nord is a song by the Algerian singer Cheb Mami and the French-Algerian rapper K-Mel. It was first recorded for Mami's eighth studio album Meli Meli. A remixed version appeared in 1998 as a single on Virgin Records and became a great success. In France the single reached number 5 on the SNEP chart and in Wallonia number 8, and it became one of the defining French hits of 1998 and 1999.

In the late 1990s the fusion of traditional Algerian raï with French hip hop and R&B was very popular in France, a hybrid often called raï'n'B. Parisien du Nord is one of the best-known examples. The production was by Pascal Perez, known as Imhotep, the beatmaker of the Marseille hip-hop group IAM. The beat contains samples of Funk You Up by The Sequence and Change the Beat (French Rap) by Beside.

In the lyrics the socially aware French raps of K-Mel, about the struggle and identity problems of North African immigrants in France, alternate with Mami's wistful, floating Arabic singing in the chorus. The subject is immigration, racism and the feeling of being a stranger in one's own country. As a result the song appealed to many young French people with Maghrebi roots.
artiest/cheb-mami-en-k-mel.listen: Listen to Parisien du Nord. Notice the interplay between the rap in French and the high Arabic singing in the chorus, and how the beat keeps running underneath.

artiest/cheikha-rimitti.text: Cheikha Rimitti, born as Saadia El Ghizania in Tessala in western Algeria, made her first record in 1952. She sang in street language about longing, drink and poverty, subjects that until then had been heard only privately at weddings, and her hit Charrak Gatta shocked conservative listeners. Younger raï singers called her the mother of the genre. On Sidi Mansour (1994) Flea and Robert Fripp played with her.
artiest/cheikha-rimitti.listen: Listen to Charragt, a later recording of her early hit: her raw voice is up front, carried by a stomping rhythm.

artiest/cher.text:
Cher was born in 1946 as Cheryl Sarkisian in El Centro, California. Her father was Armenian-American and her mother was a model and actress. The family moved often and had little money. Even as a child Cher had a striking low voice and dreamed of becoming famous. At sixteen she left school and tried to break into Hollywood.

In 1965 she broke through with Sonny Bono as the duo Sonny & Cher. Their hit I Got You Babe became a symbol of the 1960s. At the same time she began a solo career, with dramatic pop songs such as Bang Bang (My Baby Shot Me Down). In the 1970s came narrative hits such as Gypsys, Tramps & Thieves, Half-Breed and Dark Lady, and she had popular television shows. After that she also became an actress and won an Oscar for Moonstruck. In the late 1980s she opted for hard rock, with If I Could Turn Back Time.

In 1998, at the age of 52, she made the dance album Believe. In the title track Auto-Tune, a program intended to correct wrong notes unobtrusively, was set up precisely so that her voice jumped audibly mechanically from note to note. That sound was named the Cher effect and was afterwards imitated everywhere in pop and hip hop. Believe became her biggest hit. Cher remained active for more than six decades by continually reinventing herself, and committed herself to gay rights and the fight against AIDS.
artiest/cher.listen: Listen to Believe. Notice Cher's voice in the verses: on some words it jumps like a robot from note to note. That is Auto-Tune, deliberately exaggerated.

artiest/cherie-currie.text:
Cherie Currie was born in 1959 and grew up in Encino, California. She is an American singer, musician, actress and artist. With her twin sister Marie she appeared on television as a child and later danced as a background dancer on American Bandstand. In 1975, at the age of fifteen, she joined The Runaways, an all-girl rock band from Los Angeles. Her bandmates were Joan Jett, Lita Ford, Sandy West, Jackie Fox and Vicki Blue. The magazine Bomp! described her as the lost daughter of Iggy Pop and Brigitte Bardot.

With The Runaways she recorded three albums: The Runaways, Queens of Noise and Live In Japan. After the third album she left the group, at the age of seventeen. To fulfil her contract she made the solo album Beauty's Only Skin Deep. She then performed in clubs in Los Angeles, where her sister Marie sometimes joined her on stage. Together they recorded the album Messin' With The Boys as Cherie & Marie Currie, whose best-known song was Since You Been Gone, a cover of a song by Russ Ballard. In 1980 she also appeared in the film Foxes. Later she released further albums, such as Reverie in 2015.

Currie was the face of one of the first rock bands of young women. Her performance showed that in the 1970s girls could sound just as hard and raw as the male rock bands, even though her group did not always receive appreciation for it.
artiest/cherie-currie.listen: Listen to Since You Been Gone by Cherie & Marie Currie and notice how the two sisters sing together. Try to hear what distinguishes this calmer rock sound from the rawer style of The Runaways.

artiest/chester-bennington.text:
Chester Bennington was an American singer and songwriter, born in 1976 in Phoenix, Arizona. From a young age he listened to Depeche Mode and Stone Temple Pilots. His childhood was hard: he was abused for years, his parents divorced and he took to drink and drugs early on. To comfort himself he drew and wrote poems and songs. His first serious band was the post-grunge group Grey Daze, with which he recorded two albums in the 1990s.

In 1999 he auditioned for a group from Los Angeles that was then still called Xero and later Linkin Park. He became the main singer, alongside Mike Shinoda, who rapped more. The debut album Hybrid Theory from 2000 was a worldwide success, with songs such as Crawling and In the End. Meteora from 2003 and Minutes to Midnight from 2007 followed, among others. Linkin Park blended heavy guitars with hip hop, samples and electronics, the style now called nu metal.

Bennington had a high, emotional voice that could switch in a single song from soft singing to raw screaming. His lyrics were often about pain, doubt and addiction. Besides Linkin Park he sang in Dead by Sunrise and for a time with his childhood heroes Stone Temple Pilots. He struggled with depression and addiction all his life and died in 2017. One critic wrote that he made nu metal universal.
artiest/chester-bennington.listen: Listen to In the End by Linkin Park. Notice the division of roles: Mike Shinoda raps the verses calmly, and in the chorus Chester Bennington takes over with a voice that grows steadily fiercer.

artiest/chet-baker.text: The trumpeter and singer Chet Baker grew up in Oklahoma and California. In 1952 he played with Charlie Parker in Los Angeles and became a member of Gerry Mulligan's quartet, with whom he recorded My Funny Valentine. His trumpet tone was soft and lyrical, his singing light and unadorned. With his looks he became an idol, the face of West Coast jazz. His album Chet Baker Sings (1954) became a classic. Baker became addicted to heroin, went to prison and lived for a long time in Europe. In 1988 he died after a fall from a hotel window in Amsterdam, where a plaque at the hotel commemorates him.
artiest/chet-baker.listen: Listen to the soft, almost whispering sound of trumpet and voice.

artiest/chic.text:
Chic is an American disco band founded in 1972 by the guitarist Nile Rodgers and the bassist Bernard Edwards. They met in 1970 as session musicians in New York, first formed a rock band, The Boys, and then The Big Apple Band, and played in the group New York City, which had a hit in 1973 with I'm Doing Fine Now. When that group broke up in 1976, they adopted the name Chic. Rodgers was inspired by a Roxy Music concert and wanted a group whose music and image formed a whole. Kiss was also an influence. They brought in the drummer Tony Thompson, the keyboard player Raymond Jones and the singer Norma Jean Wright, later joined by Luci Martin.

In 1977 the self-titled debut album Chic appeared on Atlantic Records, with Dance, Dance, Dance (Yowsah, Yowsah, Yowsah) and Everybody Dance. In 1978 came C'est Chic, with Le Freak and I Want Your Love, and in 1979 Risqué with Good Times. Real People, Take It Off and It's About Time in 2018 followed later. According to Rodgers, Chic was a rock band for the disco movement, which delivered what the hippies had promised with peace, love and freedom.

The music revolves around Rodgers's sharp, rhythmic guitar, Edwards's walking bass lines and the tight drums. The result is an elegant, danceable groove. Chic was nominated for the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame for the eleventh time in 2017 and still performs as Nile Rodgers & Chic.
artiest/chic.listen: Listen to Le Freak. Notice Rodgers's short, dry guitar chords and Edwards's driving bass line, and how those two together determine the rhythm of the whole song.

artiest/chicago-symphony-orchestra.text:
The Chicago Symphony Orchestra, CSO for short, is an American symphony orchestra in downtown Chicago. It was founded in 1891 by Theodore Thomas, at the invitation of the businessman Charles Norman Fay. The first concert was on 16 October 1891 at the Auditorium Theater. Since 1904 the orchestra has played in Orchestra Hall, part of Symphony Center, and in the summer at the Ravinia Festival. It is one of the Big Five, the five American orchestras often named as the best. It received the name Chicago Symphony Orchestra in 1913.

Successive chief conductors have shaped the orchestra. Frederick Stock led it from 1905 until his death in 1942. He was followed by, among others, Rafael Kubelík, Fritz Reiner, Jean Martinon, Georg Solti and Daniel Barenboim. Reiner made television appearances, the first in the orchestra's history. In 1971 Solti toured ten European countries with the orchestra, the first time it played outside North America. On its return home it received a ticker-tape parade. From 2010 to 2023 Riccardo Muti was chief conductor. Records released include Bartók's Concerto for Orchestra in 1956 and Debussy's Iberia in 1958.

The orchestra is known for a powerful, rich sound, especially from the brass. It plays the great symphonic repertoire, but also new music. For anyone looking at the history of pop music, it is an example of the classical world in which many pop and film composers were trained.
artiest/chicago-symphony-orchestra.listen: Listen to a recording of Bartók's Concerto for Orchestra and notice how the different orchestral groups take the lead in turn. Try to hear how the brass and the strings alternate.

artiest/chick-corea.text: The pianist Chick Corea, from the Boston area, grew up with the records of Bud Powell and Horace Silver. He played in Latin bands of Mongo Santamaría and Willie Bobo, which shaped his sense of rhythm. In 1968 he recorded the trio album Now He Sings, Now He Sobs and afterwards played electric piano with Miles Davis. In 1972 he founded Return to Forever, first with the singer Flora Purim and the percussionist Airto Moreira, later as a loud fusion band. Spain, based on the Concierto de Aranjuez, became a standard. Corea won more than twenty Grammys and also often played duets with the vibraphonist Gary Burton.
artiest/chick-corea.listen: Notice the Spanish and Latin American rhythms in the piano.

artiest/chick-webb.text:
William Henry Chick Webb was born in Baltimore, probably in 1905, and died in 1939. His exact year of birth is disputed. He was an American jazz and swing drummer and bandleader. As a baby he fell down a staircase, after which a spinal disease left him small in stature and physically limited. His doctor advised him to play an instrument to keep his bones supple. He earned money for a drum kit as a newspaper boy and gave his first professional performance at the age of eleven. At seventeen he moved to New York and by 1926 he was already leading a band of his own in Harlem.

In 1931 his orchestra became the house band of the Savoy Ballroom. There he played battle-of-the-bands contests against the orchestras of Benny Goodman and Count Basie. In 1937 he lost to Duke Ellington. Webb could not read music. He memorised the arrangements and conducted from a platform in the middle of the band, with custom-made pedals and a 28-inch bass drum. He took the young Ella Fitzgerald under his wing. She became the singer of his orchestra, and after his death in 1939 she took over the band.

Webb was regarded as one of the best drummers of the swing years. Buddy Rich called him the father of them all. The drummer showed that a percussionist could drive a whole big band, with power and ingenuity. In doing so he laid a foundation for later drummers in jazz and rock.
artiest/chick-webb.listen: Listen to a recording by Chick Webb and His Orchestra and notice the drumming that drives the band. Try to hear how the drummer sets the tempo and spurs on the horns.

artiest/chico-hamilton.text:
Foreststorn Chico Hamilton (1921 to 2013) was an American jazz drummer and bandleader from Los Angeles. He began as a schoolboy in a band with, among others, Charles Mingus and Dexter Gordon. He then played with Lionel Hampton, Lester Young, Count Basie, Duke Ellington, Billie Holiday, Gerry Mulligan and Lena Horne. In 1941 he appeared in the film You'll Never Get Rich as a member of the band behind Fred Astaire. He recorded his first album as a leader in 1955 for Pacific Jazz.

In that same year he formed a remarkable quintet in Los Angeles, with cello, flute, saxophones and clarinet, guitar, bass and drums. That the cello was given the leading voice was unusual in jazz in the 1950s. The first line-up consisted of Buddy Collette, the guitarist Jim Hall, the cellist Fred Katz and the bassist Jim Aton. The quintet was seen as one of the last important bands of West Coast jazz and appeared in the films Sweet Smell of Success from 1957 and Jazz on a Summer's Day from 1960. In 1961 Hamilton renewed his group with Charles Lloyd, Gábor Szabó, George Bohanon and Albert Stinson. That group played what has been called chamber jazz, with a moderate avant-gardism. Albums from that time are Passin' Thru and Man From Two Worlds.

Hamilton played Cool Jazz, post-bop and later jazz fusion. His significance lies in the way he built his groups: he gave young musicians such as Lloyd, Hall and Szabó room to develop. His soft, strikingly coloured line-up showed that jazz could be more than trumpets and saxophones.
artiest/chico-hamilton.listen: Listen to a track from Passin' Thru and notice the guitar, the flute and the soft, subtle drums. Try to hear how Hamilton accompanies the band with brushes and light strokes without drowning it out.

artiest/chico-o-farrill.text:
Arturo Chico O'Farrill (1921 to 2001) was a Cuban composer, arranger and conductor, best known for Afro-Cuban jazz, also called Cubop. He was born in Havana into an aristocratic family and was meant to become a lawyer. At a military boarding school in Florida he got to know big-band jazz and learned to play the trumpet. Back in Havana he studied classical music at the conservatory and played in nightclubs. In 1948 he moved to New York, where he continued his studies at the Juilliard School and also sought out the jazz scene.

Shortly after his arrival he became an arranger for Benny Goodman, for whom he wrote Undercurrent Blues. Goodman found his name hard to pronounce and called him Chico, and so his nickname came about. He then arranged for, among others, Stan Kenton, Count Basie and Art Farmer. In 1950 he wrote the Afro-Cuban Jazz Suite for Machito, recorded with Charlie Parker. He also worked on Afro-Cuban pieces by Parker and Dizzy Gillespie, such as Manteca Theme. Between 1957 and 1965 he lived in Mexico. In the 1990s he led a big band that performed at the New York club Birdland, a band later taken over by his son Arturo, a pianist.

O'Farrill linked the compelling rhythms of Cuba with the written music and colours of the jazz orchestra. His arrangements gave big-band jazz a Latin American colour. In this way he contributed to the way Cuban sounds gained a permanent place in American jazz and later in pop music.
artiest/chico-o-farrill.listen: Listen to Machito's Afro-Cuban Jazz Suite and notice the contrast between the Cuban percussion and the jazz solos of Charlie Parker. Try to hear how the horns play in short, sharp bursts.

artiest/chief-keef.text:
Chief Keef, real name Keith Farrelle Cozart, is an American rapper and producer, born in 1995 in Chicago. He grew up on the South Side, in the Washington Park district, with his grandmother, who was a school bus driver. He began rapping at the age of five with his mother's karaoke set and left school in his first year of high school. He started in 2008, released his first mixtape in 2009 and in 2011 gained local attention with mixtapes such as The Glory Road and Bang.

In December 2011 he was arrested and placed under house arrest at his grandmother's. There he posted videos on YouTube, forerunners of the Chicago hip-hop style drill. His mixtape Back from the Dead from 2012 produced I Don't Like, his first entry on the American Hot 100. After a bidding war he signed with Interscope and the song was re-released with Love Sosa, which went five-times platinum. Both were singles from the debut album Finally Rich from 2012, his only release on a major label. Later albums such as Bang 3, 4Nem and Almighty So 2 reached the Billboard 200 as independent releases.

Chief Keef is seen as someone who brought drill to a wide audience and as one of the founders of the genre. Drill sounds cold and dark, with slow, heavy beats and a deadpan, shouted delivery. He also had a guest role on Bean (Kobe) by Lil Uzi Vert and All the Parties by Drake.
artiest/chief-keef.listen: Listen to Love Sosa. Notice the dark, slow beat and the measured, almost shrugging way in which he lets his lines fall.

artiest/childish-gambino.text:
Childish Gambino is the musical stage name of Donald Glover, an American actor, rapper, singer, comedian and filmmaker. He was born in 1983 and grew up in Stone Mountain, Georgia. At New York University he studied dramatic writing, and at twenty-three he wrote for the TV series 30 Rock at the invitation of Tina Fey. Later he became known as Troy Barnes in Community and as creator and lead actor of the series Atlanta. For music he began as a DJ and producer under the name mcDJ, before making his first rap projects.

In 2011 he signed with Glassnote Records and released his debut album Camp. The second album Because the Internet appeared in 2013, with the song 3005, his first entry on the Billboard Hot 100. His third album Awaken, My Love! came in 2016, preceded by the psychedelic funk single Redbone, which won a Grammy. In 2018 This Is America topped the Hot 100. The song won four Grammys, including Record of the Year and Song of the Year, and was the first hip-hop song to win those two categories. Later came, among others, 3.15.20 in 2020 and Atavista in 2024.

Gambino's music moves between rap, funk, soul and electronics. He shows that an artist can have a voice of his own in music, television and film at once. With This Is America he brought together a music video and a song that provoked a broad discussion about America.
artiest/childish-gambino.listen: Listen to Redbone and notice the falsetto singing and the slow, funky bass line. Try to hear how this song sounds like 1970s soul, even though it dates from 2016.

artiest/chiquinha-gonzaga.text: Chiquinha Gonzaga, from Rio de Janeiro, was a pianist, composer and Brazil's first female conductor. She was the first woman to play in the choro group of the flautist Joaquim Callado, and her polka Atraente (1877) became her first great success. For the 1899 carnival she wrote Ó Abre Alas, the first carnival march. Her Corta-Jaca was played in 1914 in the presidential palace, which caused a scandal.
artiest/chiquinha-gonzaga.listen: Listen to Atraente, a polka with Brazilian swing: the melody seems European, but the accompaniment already sways like choro.

artiest/choir-of-the-russian-orthodox-ca.text:
The choir of the Russian Orthodox cathedral of Paris sings the music of the Orthodox liturgy. In the Russian tradition that music is sung without instruments: the church uses only human voices. The choir belongs to the Russian community in Paris, which received many exiles from Russia after the revolution of 1917.

We Praise You in the znamenny version is an example of the oldest layer of this music. Znamenny chant is the old liturgical monophonic chant of the Russian church, with a melody built from fixed formulas and sung in a free, calm metre. It is church music that is older than the polyphonic choral style of later centuries.

The 1993 recording shows how a choir kept this tradition alive in the West. It is not pop music, but the line of the singing, the repetition and the silence between the phrases have appealed to many listeners and helped to shape the image of what sacred music can be.
artiest/choir-of-the-russian-orthodox-ca.listen: Listen to We Praise You. Notice the simple melodic line, the absence of instruments and how the voices breathe at a calm pace.
